\begin{document}
\begin{abstract}
Noisy supervision makes a fine-tuned model memorize wrong labels. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first
filter that compares gradients inside a batch. At a noise rate of 0.2 the accuracy rises by 2.1 points (Table 2).
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
To the best of our knowledge, no earlier filter compares gradients inside a batch.
It should be noted that the reference set is small.
One might argue that 64 verified samples are too few.
We do not claim that the filter removes every noisy label.
Due to space limitations, the proofs are in Appendix B.

\section{Method}
The filter keeps sample $i$ when its cosine with the reference gradient is at least $\tau$. It is cheap.
In some cases the filter discards clean samples.
In some cases where two samples share a gradient, the filter keeps the first one.
Under mild assumptions (Assumption 2) the filtered update is a descent direction.
The cost could potentially grow with the batch.
Admittedly, the reference gradient is recomputed every 50 steps.
Stochastic rounding is beyond the scope of this paper.
To the best of our knowledge, the bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:descent} is new.
Reviewers may wonder why the threshold is fixed, and the reason might seem arbitrary. % style-exempt

\section{Experiments}
Accuracy rises by 2.1 points at a noise rate of 0.2 (Table 2), and the gain may shrink at higher noise rates.
We believe this is because the reference set itself becomes noisier.
The gap appears to be stable across five seeds. Seeds matter less than the noise rate, which sets both the size of the retained set and the share of noisy labels inside it.
Unfortunately, the largest model did not fit in memory.
We leave larger models to future work.

\section{Limitations}
We do not claim that the filter helps when the noise rate exceeds 0.4 (Table 5).
Models with more than seven billion parameters are beyond the scope of this paper.

\section{Conclusion}
The filter raises accuracy by 2.1 points at a noise rate of 0.2 (Table 2).
